teaser.text: Simon Property Group is a landlord packaged as a publicly traded company. It owns shopping destinations, leases space to businesses and turns that rental activity into income for shareholders.

stock.opening: Simon’s weighted case points to $245.03 in October 2027 and reaches $271.28 by October 2029. It hinges on turning destination strength into durable per-share earnings without letting debt consume the return.
stock.closing: The full memo also answers how Simon’s business works, who its rivals are, how management allocates capital, and what risks matter.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Simon?

paragraphs.text: The starting point is management’s $13.25 per-share 2026 guidance midpoint applied to 380.361 million diluted shares and units. First-half Real Estate FFO per share was $6.46, up 7.5% year over year, while occupancy was 96.0% and base rent per square foot rose 6.3%. The base assumes 4.5% annual per-share growth. The bear assumes declines of 2% and 3%, while the bull assumes 7% growth. Debt maturities of $5.044 billion in 2027 and $3.069 billion in 2028 explain the downside.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Simon really make?

paragraphs.text: FAD, or funds available for distribution, moves closer to cash by showing selected recurring property needs. In the first half of 2026, Simon deducted $150.7 million of tenant allowances and $107.9 million of operational capital expenditures. Tenant allowances help attract or retain tenants, while operational capital keeps properties functioning and competitive.

The bridge left FAD of $2.158 billion, but it also added back $75.3 million of stock compensation. That is not the same as cash being free of cost: if equity compensation increases the share count, existing holders bear dilution.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Simon’s earnings and cash?

paragraphs.text: Adjusted funds from operations, or AFFO, goes further by subtracting recurring costs such as tenant improvements, leasing expenses, and capital work. Neither measure is cash in the bank, and companies calculate AFFO differently. The current table shows the share price, market value, operating multiples, dividend, and share count.

blocks.heading: How much does Simon pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Simon later sold its ABG investment, receiving $1.2 billion in cash proceeds for the remaining interest. The sales created accounting gains and tax expense, so some reported results came from selling an investment rather than recurring mall rent. The board has authorized up to $2 billion of repurchases through February 2028. The quarterly dividend rose to $2.25 in May 2026 and stayed there in August. These choices lead to Simon’s next capital question: can new investment earn enough?

blocks.heading: Is Simon's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: The dividend is covered by Simon’s Real Estate FFO, but the cushion is not simply spare cash.

Simon is a REIT, a property company that generally distributes taxable income to shareholders, so dividends compete directly with investment and balance-sheet protection. In its five-year cash record, operating cash exceeded common dividends in every year.

A 68.4% Real Estate FFO payout supports moderate growth, but $5.906 billion of debt scheduled to mature in 2026 as of December 31, 2025 limits confidence in faster increases.

blocks.heading: What is Simon's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: The dividend supplies cash while investors wait for growth, but the board must declare each payment. A real-estate investment trust, or REIT, generally distributes much of its taxable income to preserve its tax status, yet property income, debt costs, vacancies, and reinvestment needs can still change future distributions.

paragraphs.text: Management guides to $13.20–$13.30 of Real Estate FFO per diluted share in 2026. The board guidance calls for common dividends of at least $8.80 per share. Simon forecasts total net cash redevelopment investment of $347,188 thousand in 2026 and $155,266 thousand in 2027. More than 60 anchor and specialty tenants are expected to open across 2026–2027.

blocks.heading: What do Simon’s last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue grew much faster than NOI against Q2 2025. The gap matters because Simon’s late-2025 Taubman consolidation changed the consolidated base, while comparable-property NOI is designed to test existing-center progress. Simon reported domestic property NOI growth of 8.5% for Q2 and said acquisitions contributed to growth, so the comparable measure remains the cleaner operating signal.

Reported FFO per share was affected by a $0.21 after-tax investment gain in Q2 2025. Real Estate FFO per share rose 7.9% year over year, which makes the recurring property comparison more useful than the reported FFO comparison. The quarter’s Real Estate FFO and dividend still need to be read alongside tenant allowances, capital spending and the longer debt schedule.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Simon’s next results?

paragraphs.text: The next scheduled checkpoint is Simon’s third-quarter 2026 earnings call on November 5, 2026. Investors should look for updates on leasing, occupancy, redevelopment spending, borrowing and the year-end outlook. Those results will begin to show whether Simon’s plan is becoming cash-generating reality.
